---
title: "Cleaning the Full Report"
---



The 4 p.m. call didn't stay about Hartford. Someone asked about
Stamford, and you didn't have it — you'd cleaned exactly one town, by
hand. The Commissioner's follow-up is blunt: **stop picking towns one at
a time. Clean the whole report once, so any town's number is ready
before the question gets asked.**

Same brief, wider net: this week's Situation Brief still leads with
Hartford, but you never want to be caught flat again when the call turns
to some other town.

## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(janitor)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(glue)

covid_data <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv"))
```
:::




## Step 1 — Clean every column name at once

Chapter 1 renamed a handful of columns by hand with `select()`. That
works for one town and four columns; it does not scale to every column
in the dataset. `clean_names()` fixes all of them in a single call.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean <-
  covid_data |>
  clean_names()

names(covid_clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "last_update_date"         "town_number"             
 [3] "town"                     "total_cases"             
 [5] "confirmed_cases"          "probable_cases"          
 [7] "case_rate"                "total_deaths"            
 [9] "confirmed_deaths"         "probable_deaths"         
[11] "people_tested"            "rate_tested_per_100k"    
[13] "number_of_tests"          "number_of_positives"     
[15] "number_of_negatives"      "number_of_indeterminates"
```


:::
:::


## Step 2 — Parse the date once, for every row


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean <-
  covid_clean |>
  mutate(last_update_date = mdy(last_update_date))

covid_clean |>
  select(last_update_date) |>
  slice(1:3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 1
  last_update_date
  <date>          
1 2022-06-24      
2 2022-06-24      
3 2022-06-24      
```


:::
:::


## Step 3 — Guard the town names with `stringr`

The town names in this file are already tidy, but a report that gets
re-downloaded every week shouldn't depend on that staying true.
Trimming whitespace and standardizing case costs nothing when the data
is already clean, and saves a debugging session the week it isn't.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean <-
  covid_clean |>
  mutate(town = town |> str_trim() |> str_to_title())
```
:::


## Step 4 — Daily new cases, for every town

Chapter 1's caveat about "as reported" data applies here at full scale.
`total_cases` is cumulative, so a daily new-case number means computing
`total_cases - lag(total_cases)` again — but this time across 169
towns at once, which means grouping by `town` first. Without the
`group_by()`, `lag()` would subtract the last row of one town from the
first row of the next.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean <-
  covid_clean |>
  arrange(town, last_update_date) |>
  group_by(town) |>
  mutate(new_cases = total_cases - lag(total_cases)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::


Chapter 1 warned this could happen; at 169 towns, now it actually does.
Go look:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean |>
  filter(new_cases < 0) |>
  select(town, last_update_date, new_cases) |>
  arrange(new_cases) |>
  head()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  town         last_update_date new_cases
  <chr>        <date>               <dbl>
1 Wethersfield 2021-02-15             -97
2 Montville    2020-06-18             -88
3 Pomfret      2021-12-02             -55
4 Wethersfield 2021-02-11             -44
5 Greenwich    2021-09-13             -27
6 Groton       2020-05-24             -23
```


:::
:::


Those negative "new case" counts are real rows in your own output, not a
bug you introduced. Each one is a day a town's cumulative total came in
*lower* than its previous report — a correction, a de-duplicated test, a
late reversal. Subtracting two "as of" snapshots faithfully records that
as negative growth.

So what do you do with them? **Not** silently floor them to zero — that
hides a real data-quality signal, and the brief is supposed to be honest.
You leave them in and you don't let a single day drive a conclusion. That
is exactly why every verdict in this book averages over a week: one
corrected report can't flip the answer when it's one of seven. Knowing
these rows exist is the fix; the weekly average is the guard rail.

## Step 5 — Scope to the latest report


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
latest_date <- max(covid_clean$last_update_date)

this_week <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(last_update_date == latest_date)

nrow(this_week)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 169
```


:::
:::


## Step 6 — Generate a one-line summary per town with `glue`

This is the payoff, and the answer to the ask that opened the chapter.
The next time the call turns to Stamford — or any of the other 168 towns
— the sentence is already sitting there, no filter to re-run under
pressure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
town_lines <-
  this_week |>
  mutate(
    line = glue(
      "{town}: {total_cases} total cases ({new_cases} new), {total_deaths} deaths"
    )
  ) |>
  select(town, line)

town_lines |>
  filter(town %in% c("Hartford", "Stamford", "New Haven")) |>
  pull(line)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Hartford: 33844 total cases (22 new), 417 deaths
New Haven: 35872 total cases (24 new), 289 deaths
Stamford: 31230 total cases (36 new), 385 deaths
```


:::
:::


## Step 7 — A weekly trend appendix with `tidyr`

The Commissioner also wants to see the trend, not just the latest
snapshot, for the state's largest cities. `floor_date()` groups rows
into weeks, and `pivot_wider()` lays those weeks out as columns — a
compact table that reads left-to-right like a trend line.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cities_of_interest <- c("Hartford", "New Haven", "Bridgeport", "Stamford", "Waterbury")

weekly_trend <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town %in% cities_of_interest) |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(last_update_date, "week")) |>
  group_by(town, week) |>
  summarise(avg_new_cases = mean(new_cases, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

weekly_trend |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = week,
    values_from = avg_new_cases,
    names_prefix = "week_of_"
  ) |>
  clean_names()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  town       week_of_2020_03_22 week_of_2020_03_29 week_of_2020_04_05
  <chr>                   <dbl>              <dbl>              <dbl>
1 Bridgeport               6.5                15.4               75.7
2 Hartford                 3.5                13.9               33.1
3 New Haven                7.75               19.6               51.7
4 Stamford                13                  74                 91.6
5 Waterbury                7                  25.6               39  
# ℹ 115 more variables: week_of_2020_04_12 <dbl>, week_of_2020_04_19 <dbl>,
#   week_of_2020_04_26 <dbl>, week_of_2020_05_03 <dbl>,
#   week_of_2020_05_10 <dbl>, week_of_2020_05_17 <dbl>,
#   week_of_2020_05_24 <dbl>, week_of_2020_05_31 <dbl>,
#   week_of_2020_06_07 <dbl>, week_of_2020_06_14 <dbl>,

```

:::


## Putting it together

Each step above modified `covid_clean` and saved it back. Written as
one pipeline, the whole cleaning pass is:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covid_clean <-
  covid_data |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    last_update_date = mdy(last_update_date),
    town = town |> str_trim() |> str_to_title()
  ) |>
  arrange(town, last_update_date) |>
  group_by(town) |>
  mutate(new_cases = total_cases - lag(total_cases)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::


## Saving our data artifact


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# write_csv(covid_clean, here("data", "processed", "covid_clean.csv"))
```
:::


Every future chapter can now start from `covid_clean` instead of
re-deriving it — one clean pass, reused everywhere.
